{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mo-f","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"e32b3a1ae13944eedcbb290c90b00dea21b5addd1eac64fab0936dddd60938c6","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mo-class-f:lineage:46","source_registry_sha256":"f128002157e581eb7004b9370c8cfbafd7b29a1596262980704fbda0a45932f5","source_liveness_sha256":"fdf72d02e75b9589fee5aaf5b83ec9705ff03586f574464e3553a827f9b698d8"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Special driving conditions look-alikes: beam distances, pumping versus steady braking, hydroplaning speeds, and emergency step contrasts","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: the three headlight distances, pumping versus anti-lock braking, hydroplaning thresholds, following gaps, blowout versus steering failure, and emergency extras","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: the three headlight distances, pumping versus anti-lock braking, hydroplaning thresholds, following gaps, blowout versus steering failure, and emergency extras
Confusable pairs among the special driving conditions rules, plus continuation facts that complete part C; each block ties to one guide page, the skid diagram is a picture and is not described beyond its caption, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec11-R01 | anchor: A01
Three night distances are easy to mix up: headlights reach about 350 feet, you dim for oncoming traffic at 500 feet, and you dim when following within 300 feet. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; confusable beam distances; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R02 | anchor: A01
Headlights are required by the clock from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, and also by the weather whenever the wipers are needed. [A01]
Why it matters: group headlights; confusable time rule versus wiper rule; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R03 | anchor: A02
On very slippery surfaces the winter page says to pump the brakes, but for a vehicle with anti-lock brakes it points you to the owner's manual for special situations. [A02]
Why it matters: group braking; confusable pumping versus anti-lock; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-R04 | anchor: A03
Brake failure is the one emergency here where you pump the pedal fast and hard, which is the opposite of the steady pressure used with working anti-lock brakes. [A03]
Why it matters: group braking; confusable brake failure versus anti-lock stop; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-R05 | anchor: A02
Hydroplaning can begin above 35 mph, while full loss of road contact in a severe storm can come at 55 mph. [A02]
Why it matters: group hydroplaning; confusable onset versus full loss; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-R06 | anchor: A02
On snow or ice the safe gap to the vehicle ahead grows to about eight to ten seconds, because stopping takes longer. [A02]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable with the three second rule of the everyday driving chapter; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-R07 | anchor: A04
After a blowout you brake only when nearly stopped, and after a steering failure you also wait to brake until nearly stopped unless you must. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; confusable blowout versus steering failure; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R08 | anchor: A04
A stuck accelerator calls for shifting to neutral and braking right away, unlike a blowout, where you avoid the brakes at first. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; confusable stuck accelerator versus blowout; difficulty high.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R09 | anchor: A01
Slow down for curves at night if you are already driving at the posted maximum. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; continuation of night tips.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R10 | anchor: A01
Stay awake and alert at night and do not drive if you feel tired. [A01]
Why it matters: group night driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R11 | anchor: A01
Before winter driving, make sure the windshield wipers and defroster both work. [A01]
Why it matters: group winter driving; continuation of winter preparation.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R12 | anchor: A01
If your vehicle lacks snow-rated tires, keep chains ready to put on in bad weather. [A01]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R13 | anchor: A01
When starting out on snow or ice, accelerate slowly and smoothly. [A01]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec11-R14 | anchor: A02
Wet pavement also makes it harder to stay on the road through curves. [A02]
Why it matters: group wet pavement; continuation of wet pavement risks.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec11-R15 | anchor: A03
The guide's skid diagram is captioned in four steps: before the skid, rear wheels sliding right, front wheels turned right, and the vehicle straight again. [A03]
Why it matters: group skids; picture caption only; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-R16 | anchor: A03
Staying calm in an emergency helps you remember what to do. [A03]
Why it matters: group emergencies; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec11-R17 | anchor: A04
A blowout may announce itself with a loud bang followed by a repeated thumping, and the steering wheel may jerk. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; glossary blowout warning signs.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R18 | anchor: A04
When wheels run off the paved edge, they may pull to the right, so hold the wheel firmly and use only gentle braking if any is needed. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; continuation of running off the pavement.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R19 | anchor: A04
With a stuck accelerator, keep looking for a way out of traffic while you slow down. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; continuation of stuck accelerator.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R20 | anchor: A04
Swerving into the left lane to avoid a head-on vehicle is dangerous because the other driver may move back into that same lane. [A04]
Why it matters: group emergencies; continuation of head-on response.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec11-R21 | anchor: A05
Running in the direction the train is heading after a stall puts you in the path of debris when the train strikes your vehicle. [A05]
Why it matters: group railroad; confusable run toward versus away; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec11-R22 | anchor: A05
The NTSB points drivers of large passenger vans to its website for more on van safety. [A05]
Why it matters: group passenger vans; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0068]
